evidence: A runnable calculation of independent single drops through the rain product's columns, the same solver that reproduces 34 Gunn-Kinzer fall speeds on Earth: the arriving populations are the bounded cloud-base spectra filtered by evaporation below a parcel cloud base in still air, and the drips are short falls from rest. The spectra and the drips' sizes and heights are scenario boundary conditions.
reading_rule: Diameters are volume-equivalent, in mm; speeds are downward at the ground in still air, in m/s. For each target and world, classes gives each cloud-base size class's fall: whether it reaches the ground, its size and speed there and its time aloft. Each spectrum's ground_flux_per_mm_h gives, class by class, the drops arriving per square metre per second for each mm/h of rain at the ground: multiply by the ground rain rate. cloud_base_rain_per_ground_rain is the rain leaving the cloud base that each mm/h at the ground takes, 1 / water_survival_fraction; a spectrum delivering no water has null fluxes. drips gives, by release diameter and height, the size and speed at the ground of a drop released at rest; tail gives the falls of 8-12 mm drops from the cloud base, absent where they exceed the stability screen.
assumptions: The columns, airs and spectra are the rain product's (results/rain_drops.json): each target's 2 m air, the dry adiabat and fixed vapour below a parcel cloud base, still air, and the bounded gamma spectra on 64 classes from 0.1 to 6 mm.

Drops fall independently, so the arriving spectrum keeps its shape at any rain rate. The rain product's encounter diagnostic finds that on the Moon every surviving drop meets more than one other on the way down, so collisions and coalescence would reshape it, and at the rates of a shower the rain's own moistening of the air would let more water through than this column does.

Drips start at rest in the 2 m air and lose at most 2% of their water on the way down; their sizes, heights and the share of the rain that drips are left to the consumer, pending the canopy's interception and storage (biosphere/canopy).
The tail's drops leave the cloud base at their terminal speed, like the spectra's; how common they are is not computed.
